title: Wild casualty — adult buzzard: found unable to fly, weak and green-staining
presentation: Adult common buzzard brought in by a member of the public after being found grounded beside a game estate. Weak, unable to fly, bright green urates, and markedly thin.

stages.title: Assess the casualty
stages.briefing: Weight 620 g against an expected 800–1,000 g, keel sharp. Weak grip bilaterally, wings droop, unable to stand for long. No fractures on palpation, no wounds. Urates bright green. Crop empty. Pupils responsive, mild head tremor. Found near a game estate at the end of the shooting season.
stages.prompt: Which findings point to a toxic rather than a traumatic cause?

options.label: Weakness with no fractures or wounds on examination
options.detail: A grounded raptor without injury needs another explanation

options.label: Bright green urates
options.detail: Biliverdinuria from haemolysis and hepatic insult

options.label: Head tremor with bilateral weak grip
options.detail: A symmetrical neurological deficit, not a one-sided injury

options.label: Marked emaciation
options.detail: Tells you how long, not what caused it

options.label: Empty crop
options.detail: Expected in any bird that has not hunted

stages.explanation: A grounded bird of prey with no injuries and symmetrical neurological signs has been poisoned or starved, and green urates point at haemolysis with hepatic involvement. The location is the clue that makes lead top of the list: raptors ingest shotgun pellets and bullet fragments in the carcasses they scavenge. Emaciation is the consequence of days of not hunting.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: The bird is stabilised in a warm, dark box with fluids. Diagnostic imaging and laboratory work are available.

options.label: Whole-body radiographs
options.detail: Metallic fragments in the ventriculus or gut

options.label: Blood lead concentration
options.detail: The confirmatory measurement

options.label: Packed cell volume with a blood smear
options.detail: Anaemia and basophilic stippling of red cells

options.label: Biochemistry with uric acid, AST and bile acids
options.detail: Renal and hepatic effect of the toxin and of starvation

options.label: Faecal parasitology and a crop wash
options.detail: Concurrent trichomoniasis and parasitism are common in casualties

options.label: Organophosphate cholinesterase assay as the first-line test
options.detail: A reasonable differential for a poisoned raptor, but the green urates and setting point at lead

options.label: Post-release satellite tagging arrangements
options.detail: Not a diagnostic test

stages.explanation: Radiographs and a blood lead run together because either alone misleads: lead can have passed through the gizzard and left no metal to see, while a metal density in a grit-eating bird is not proof of toxicosis. The smear adds supportive evidence for free, and the parasitology reflects the reality that wildlife casualties usually have more than one problem.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Radiographs: two small metallic densities in the ventriculus. Blood lead 2.9 ppm (toxic above 0.6 ppm in raptors). PCV 26% (ref 37–53); smear shows basophilic stippling with mild anisocytosis. Uric acid 820 µmol/L (raised), AST raised, bile acids mildly raised. Crop wash: no Trichomonas. Faecal: light Capillaria burden. Cholinesterase not measured.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Lead toxicosis with anaemia
options.detail: Blood lead 2.9 ppm with stippling and a PCV of 26%

options.label: Retained metallic fragments are an ongoing source
options.detail: Two densities still in the ventriculus

options.label: Dehydration and starvation are compounding the azotaemia
options.detail: Raised uric acid in an emaciated bird with an empty crop

options.label: A light Capillaria burden needs treating, but it is not the reason it was grounded
options.detail: Incidental in the context of a lead of 2.9 ppm

options.label: The metal densities alone prove toxicosis
options.detail: Grit and shot fragments occur in well birds; the blood lead is what proves it

options.label: Organophosphate poisoning remains the leading diagnosis
options.detail: Unmeasured and unnecessary — lead is confirmed at a toxic concentration

stages.explanation: The blood lead is what converts two specks on a radiograph into a diagnosis, and the distinction matters because raptors swallow grit and inert debris routinely. Basophilic stippling and the anaemia show the toxin has been at work for a while, and the raised uric acid is starvation and dehydration rather than a second disease — which changes how you fluid-load before chelating.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Blood lead 2.9 ppm, metallic densities in the ventriculus, PCV 26% with basophilic stippling, raised uric acid from starvation and dehydration, no Trichomonas, light Capillaria burden.

options.label: Lead toxicosis from ingested ammunition fragments, with anaemia and starvation
options.detail: Confirmed toxic lead with its source and consequences

options.label: Trauma from a collision
options.detail: No fractures, no wounds, and symmetrical deficits

options.label: Trichomoniasis
options.detail: Crop wash negative

options.label: Organophosphate toxicosis
options.detail: Lead is confirmed at a toxic level and explains every finding

options.label: Starvation alone
options.detail: Does not produce stippling, green urates or a lead of 2.9 ppm

stages.explanation: The diagnosis sets a sequence: rehydrate and feed before chelation, remove or allow passage of the fragments, chelate with sodium calcium edetate, then reassess the lead before considering release. It also generates a report — lead in a scavenging raptor beside a shoot is a population issue, and casualty records are how that evidence is built.
